start.display: in operation by 2005; commissioning date not sourced

summary.plain: A rapid-cycling ring 474 metres around that takes protons to 8 billion electronvolts. It feeds the Booster neutrino beam and the rest of the Fermilab chain.

start.display: in operation by 2005; commissioning date not sourced

summary.plain: The first machine in the Fermilab chain: it turns hydrogen ions into a 400-million-electronvolt beam and passes them to the next accelerator.

start.display: in operation by 2005; commissioning date not sourced

summary.plain: A 3.3-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 120 billion electronvolts. Its beam makes the NuMI neutrinos today and will make the LBNF beam for DUNE.
A new 215-metre superconducting accelerator being built at Fermilab. It will replace the old first-stage machine and let the laboratory make the most intense high-energy neutrino beam in the world.

intervals.label: proton stacking for the NuMI programme

start.display: in this role from the 2013 NuMI restart

summary.plain: A fixed-energy storage ring sitting in the same tunnel as the Main Injector. It stacks protons while the Main Injector accelerates, so the neutrino beam can be made faster.
The proton-antiproton collider that was the most powerful in the world until the LHC. It ran at Fermilab until 2011 and was where the top quark was found.

A major upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider now being installed. By replacing about 1.2 kilometres of the ring with new magnets and equipment it will squeeze the beams harder so that many more collisions happen each second, giving the experiments roughly ten times more data.

The world's first machine to collide two beams of protons head-on, built at CERN and running from 1971 to 1984. It convinced physicists that colliding hadrons could work, and it held the record for collision rate among hadron colliders until 2004.
The first machine in the J-PARC chain: a 300-metre linear accelerator that gives hydrogen ions their initial energy before they are passed to the ring accelerators.

intervals.label: shutdown after the Great East Japan Earthquake
operation at 760 kW after the 2023 beamline upgrade

summary.plain: The largest J-PARC accelerator: a 1.6-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 30 billion electronvolts and fires them at the target that makes the neutrino beam.
A fast-cycling ring that takes protons from the linac up to 3 billion electronvolts 25 times a second, feeding both a neutron source and the main ring.

KEK's first big accelerator, a proton ring finished in 1976. From 1999 it produced the neutrino beam for K2K, the first experiment to send neutrinos hundreds of kilometres to a distant detector. Experiments ended in 2005.

intervals.label: shut down for the SuperKEKB upgrade

summary.plain: A three-kilometre-long machine at the KEK laboratory in Japan that smashed electrons into positrons at different energies from 1998 to 2010. It made huge numbers of B mesons for the Belle experiment and set a world record for collision rate.

The largest electron-positron collider ever built: a 27-kilometre ring under the Swiss-French border that ran from 1989 to 2000 and produced about 17 million Z particles. Its tunnel was then reused for the Large Hadron Collider.

The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator: a 27-kilometre ring of superconducting magnets under the Swiss-French border that steers two beams of protons in opposite directions and smashes them together inside four large experiments, including ATLAS.

The straight accelerator that started every proton used in CERN's experiments for forty years. It took protons up to 50 million electronvolts and passed them to the Proton Synchrotron Booster, and it was switched off for the last time in November 2018.

An 86-metre straight accelerator, 12 metres underground, that is the first step for every proton used at CERN. It accelerates hydrogen ions to 160 million electronvolts and has been the source of the beams that end up in the Large Hadron Collider since 2020.

CERN's oldest working accelerator, a 628-metre ring that first accelerated protons in 1959. For a short time it was the most powerful accelerator in the world, and it still feeds every beam that ends up in the Large Hadron Collider.

intervals.label: Linac2 era (50 MeV in, 1.4 GeV out)

summary.plain: Four small accelerator rings stacked on top of each other that take particles from the linear accelerator and give them their first big push before the Proton Synchrotron. Adding the Booster in 1972 let CERN put more than a hundred times as many protons into the next machine.

A seven-kilometre ring at CERN that has been the laboratory's workhorse since 1976. It accelerates protons to 450 billion electronvolts and hands them to the Large Hadron Collider, and in the 1980s it was rebuilt to collide protons with antiprotons, which is how the W and Z particles were discovered.

specs.collision_scheme: nano-beam scheme with a large crossing angle at the interaction point

summary.plain: The rebuilt version of the KEKB collider in Japan. It squeezes its electron and positron beams down to nanometre thinness so they collide far more often than before, and since 2020 it has held the world record for collision rate.

beamline:bnb.direction: on-axis toward the short-baseline detector halls on the Fermilab site, about 500 m from the target

summary.plain: A low-energy neutrino beam at Fermilab made by firing 8-billion-electronvolt protons at a beryllium target. It feeds the short-baseline detectors on the laboratory site.

beamline:j-parc-neutrino.direction: Bent 80.7 degrees in the arc section towards the direction of Kamioka, then under the main island of Japan to Super-Kamiokande

beamline:j-parc-neutrino.name: J-PARC neutrino beamline

summary.plain: The beamline that turns J-PARC's proton beam into neutrinos: protons hit a graphite rod, magnetic "horns" focus the particles produced, and they decay in flight into neutrinos aimed slightly off to one side of the detectors 295 km away.

beamline:kek-neutrino.name: KEK neutrino beamline (K2K)
beamline:kek-neutrino.secondary_beam: Muon neutrinos, on-axis, mean energy about 1.5 GeV

summary.plain: The beamline at KEK that made the world's first accelerator neutrino beam aimed at a detector hundreds of kilometres away: 12 GeV protons on an aluminium rod, two magnetic horns, and a 200-metre pipe in which the particles decayed into neutrinos.

beamline:kek-neutrino.target: Aluminium rod, 66 cm long and 3 cm in diameter, inside the first of two focusing horns

beamline:lbnf.direction: from Fermilab (Batavia, Illinois) north-west through the Earth to SURF (Lead, South Dakota); no tunnel is required
beamline:lbnf.name: Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF) beamline
beamline:lbnf.secondary_beam: muon neutrinos / antineutrinos, on-axis, wide band

summary.plain: The facility being built at Fermilab to fire the world’s most intense beam of high-energy neutrinos 1285 kilometres through the Earth to South Dakota, plus the huge caverns that hold the detectors.

beamline:numi.direction: north-west from Fermilab, inclined 58 mrad (3.34 degrees) downward to point at the Soudan mine in Minnesota, 734 km away
beamline:numi.name: NuMI (Neutrinos at the Main Injector) beamline
beamline:numi.secondary_beam: muon neutrinos / antineutrinos from a 675 m decay volume; on-axis for MINOS/MINOS+/MINERvA, 14.6 mrad off-axis for NOvA

summary.plain: Fermilab’s long-running neutrino beam. Protons hit a graphite target and the particles that come out decay into neutrinos aimed at detectors in Minnesota.

beamline:numi.target: graphite target approximately 1 m in length

summary.plain: The international team of about 300 physicists who built and ran the ALEPH detector at CERN's LEP collider.

The international team that built and runs the ATLAS experiment. It counts its birthday as 1 October 1992, the day it handed CERN its Letter of Intent, and today it has more than 5500 members from over 170 institutions in about 40 countries.
The international team of physicists who built and ran the Belle detector at the KEK laboratory in Japan and analysed its data.
The worldwide team running the Belle II experiment in Japan: more than 1100 scientists and engineers from 122 institutions in 27 countries.
The international team that built and runs the CMS experiment: several thousand physicists, engineers and students from hundreds of universities and laboratories in more than sixty countries.
The international team of about 550 physicists from 56 institutes who built and ran the DELPHI detector at CERN's LEP collider.
The international team of more than 1500 scientists and engineers, from 228 institutions in 38 countries, that designs, builds and will run the DUNE experiment.
The international team building Hyper-Kamiokande: about 680 researchers who have taken part from over 140 institutes in 23 countries.
The international team, originally led by Nobel laureate Carlo Rubbia, that built the ICARUS liquid-argon detector, ran it in Italy, rebuilt it at CERN, and now runs it at Fermilab.
The international team that runs the IceCube telescope at the South Pole: about 450 scientists at 58 universities and laboratories in 14 countries. It grew out of the earlier AMANDA team in 1999.
The Japan-Korea-US team that built and ran K2K, the world's first long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment, from 1999 to 2004.
The international team who built and ran the L3 detector at CERN's LEP collider, drawing on institutes across roughly 22 countries.
The international team of about 250 scientists from 39 institutions in six countries that built and runs the LZ dark matter detector in South Dakota.
The team that built and ran the MicroBooNE liquid-argon detector at Fermilab, and continues to analyse its data to search for new kinds of neutrinos.
The team that built and ran the MINERvA neutrino-nucleus cross-section experiment at Fermilab, and continues to publish analyses of its data.
The team, co-led by Janet Conrad and Bill Louis, that built and ran the MiniBooNE detector at Fermilab from 2002 to 2019 to test a puzzling earlier neutrino result.
The physicists who built and ran the MINOS experiment, and its follow-on run MINOS+, sending a neutrino beam from Fermilab to a detector 735 kilometres away in Minnesota from 2005 to 2016.
The 203 scientists and engineers, from 53 institutions in nine countries, who built and run the NOvA neutrino experiment.
The international team of about 200 physicists from 34 institutes who built and ran the OPAL detector at CERN's LEP collider.

Not one experiment but a joint programme: three liquid-argon detectors (ICARUS, SBND, and originally MicroBooNE) sharing Fermilab's Booster neutrino beam to hunt for a possible fourth kind of neutrino.
The roughly 250 physicists and engineers from 38 institutions in five countries who built and run the SBND detector.
The international team of about 240 physicists from roughly 60 institutions in 11 countries who run the Super-Kamiokande detector.
The international team of about 560 physicists from roughly 75 institutions in 14 countries (plus CERN) who built and run the T2K experiment.
The international team of physicists and engineers, led by Carlo Rubbia, who built and ran the UA1 detector at CERN and co-discovered the W and Z bosons.
The international team of physicists who built and ran the UA2 detector at CERN, co-discovering the W and Z bosons with the UA1 Collaboration.

detector:aleph.name: ALEPH detector

specs.calorimeters: Electromagnetic calorimeter to identify electrons and photons; hadron calorimeter to detect hadrons

subsystems.description: 4.4 m long, 3.6 m in diameter, the central charged-particle tracker.

detector:aleph.technology: General-purpose collider detector with a large-volume time projection chamber inside a superconducting solenoid

detector:atlas.name: ATLAS detector

specs.tracker: Silicon pixel detector (92 million pixels, innermost layer 3.3 cm from the beam), semiconductor tracker (about 4000 modules, 6 million silicon micro-strips over 60 m^2) and transition radiation tracker (300 000 thin-walled drift tubes)

subsystems.description: Pixel detector, semiconductor tracker and transition radiation tracker inside the 2 T solenoid, reconstructing charged-particle tracks and vertices for |eta| < 2.5
subsystems.name: Inner Detector

subsystems.description: Accordion-geometry lead/liquid-argon sampling calorimeter measuring electron and photon energies; barrel 6.4 m long, 53 cm thick, 110 000 channels, held at -184 C
subsystems.name: Liquid-argon electromagnetic calorimeter

subsystems.description: Steel and plastic-scintillator sampling calorimeter of about 420 000 tiles and 9500 photomultipliers weighing almost 2900 tonnes, measuring hadron and jet energies in the barrel region
subsystems.name: Tile hadronic calorimeter

subsystems.description: Three layers of precision chambers in the air-core toroid field, including 1171 monitored-drift-tube chambers with 354 240 tubes, and wheels 25 m in diameter at each end
subsystems.name: Muon spectrometer

subsystems.description: Central superconducting solenoid giving 2 T in 4.5 cm of material with 38 MJ stored energy, a 25.3 m long barrel toroid of eight coils with 1.08 GJ stored, and two end-cap toroids with 0.25 GJ each
subsystems.name: Magnet system

subsystems.description: Two-stage trigger selecting interesting collisions out of up to 1.7 billion per second and writing about 1000 events per second to storage, with the first-level decision taken in under 2.5 microseconds
subsystems.name: Trigger and data acquisition

summary.plain: A cylinder 46 metres long and 25 metres across weighing 7000 tonnes - the largest particle detector ever built. Layers of tracking chambers, calorimeters and muon chambers wrap around the point where the two proton beams meet, so that almost everything produced in a collision leaves a trace somewhere.

detector:atlas.technology: General-purpose 4-pi collider detector with a thin superconducting solenoid around the inner-detector cavity and three large superconducting air-core toroids around the calorimeters

detector:belle.name: Belle detector

summary.plain: The large barrel-shaped particle detector that surrounded the collision point of the KEKB machine from 1999 to 2010. A powerful magnet bent the tracks of the particles produced so that their momenta could be measured.

detector:belle.technology: general-purpose 4π magnetic spectrometer built around a 1.5 T superconducting solenoid

detector:belle-ii.name: Belle II detector

subsystems.description: Two layers of pixelated silicon sensors immediately around the beam pipe, measuring decay-vertex positions. A new, fully implemented pixel detector was installed during Long Shutdown 1.
subsystems.name: PXD — pixel vertex detector

subsystems.description: Four layers of double-sided silicon strip sensors surrounding the PXD.
subsystems.name: SVD — silicon vertex detector

subsystems.description: The main tracking device: a large gas volume strung with sense and field wires that measures charged-particle trajectories, momenta and specific ionisation (dE/dx).
subsystems.name: CDC — central drift chamber

subsystems.description: A barrel-shaped array of quartz-radiator Cherenkov counters used for charged-hadron identification.
subsystems.name: TOP — time-of-propagation counters

subsystems.description: A ring-imaging Cherenkov counter with an aerogel radiator in the forward end-cap, complementing the TOP for particle identification.
subsystems.name: ARICH — aerogel ring-imaging Cherenkov counter

subsystems.description: Scintillator crystals inside the solenoid that measure the energies of photons and electrons.
subsystems.name: ECL — electromagnetic calorimeter

subsystems.description: The instrumented iron flux return outside the solenoid, which detects long-lived neutral kaons and identifies muons.
subsystems.name: KLM — K-long and muon detector

summary.plain: The detector that records what comes out of the SuperKEKB collisions. Seven layers of instruments, wrapped in a strong magnet, track and identify the particles produced when electrons and positrons annihilate.

detector:belle-ii.technology: general-purpose 4π magnetic spectrometer with seven subdetectors inside a 1.5 T superconducting solenoid

detector:cms.name: CMS detector

specs.calorimeters: lead-tungstate (PbWO4) scintillating-crystal electromagnetic calorimeter and brass-scintillator sampling hadron calorimeter, with forward sampling calorimeters
specs.muon_system: four stations of muon detectors instrumenting the iron flux-return yoke: drift tubes and resistive plate chambers in the barrel, cathode strip chambers, resistive plate chambers and GEM chambers in the endcaps

subsystems.description: The largest superconducting magnet ever built; its coils and iron return yoke dominate the detector mass and the yoke is 14 m in diameter.
subsystems.name: Superconducting solenoid

subsystems.description: All-silicon pixel and strip tracker covering an area the size of a tennis court with 135 million readout channels and ~10 µm single-point accuracy.
subsystems.name: Silicon tracker

subsystems.description: Lead-tungstate (PbWO4) scintillating crystals that stop electrons and photons and measure their energy.
subsystems.name: Electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL)

subsystems.description: Brass and scintillator sampling calorimeter that stops hadrons passing through the ECAL.
subsystems.name: Hadron calorimeter (HCAL)

subsystems.description: 1400 muon chambers embedded in the steel return yoke: drift tubes, cathode strip chambers, resistive plate chambers and GEM chambers.
subsystems.name: Muon system

subsystems.description: A two-level trigger reduces the 40 MHz bunch-crossing rate to about 100 kHz at Level-1 and to about 100 events per second after the High-Level Trigger.
subsystems.name: Trigger and data acquisition

summary.plain: A 21-metre-long, 14 000-tonne particle detector wrapped around one of the points where the Large Hadron Collider's proton beams cross. Its huge magnet bends the paths of the particles produced so that their momenta can be measured.

detector:cms.technology: general-purpose 4π collider detector built around a 3.8 T superconducting solenoid, with an all-silicon tracker, a lead-tungstate crystal electromagnetic calorimeter, a brass/scintillator sampling hadron calorimeter and muon detectors in the iron flux-return yoke

detector:delphi.name: DELPHI detector

specs.tracker: Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) detectors for full charged-particle identification, plus a high-precision silicon vertex detector

subsystems.name: Ring Imaging Cherenkov (RICH) system

subsystems.description: Advanced silicon tracking for precise detection of very short-lived particles.
subsystems.name: Silicon vertex detector

summary.plain: A roughly 10-metre cube of instruments at LEP's Point 8, famous for being able to tell exactly which kind of charged particle flew through it using rings of light (Cherenkov radiation).

detector:delphi.technology: General-purpose collider detector with Ring Imaging Cherenkov particle identification and precision silicon vertexing

detector:dune-far-detector-1.name: DUNE Far Detector Module 1 (horizontal drift)

subsystems.description: Photon detectors supplementing the TPC and extending the physics reach

detector:dune-far-detector-2.technology: vertical-drift liquid argon time projection chamber with a horizontal cathode bisecting the detector and charge readout planes above and below

subsystems.name: SAND

summary.plain: A set of smaller detectors on the Fermilab site, right where the neutrino beam is made. Measuring the beam before it travels lets scientists work out what changed by the time it reaches South Dakota.

detector:dune-near-detector.technology: composite near detector: a modular liquid argon TPC (ND-LAr), a muon spectrometer downstream of it, and a magnetised on-axis beam monitor (SAND)

detector:hyper-kamiokande.name: Hyper-Kamiokande detector

subsystems.description: Up to 10,000 smaller (8 cm-class) photosensors instrumenting the outer veto region.

detector:hyper-kamiokande.technology: Large cylindrical water Cherenkov tank, the successor design to Super-Kamiokande, instrumented with new high-sensitivity large-aperture PMTs and multi-PMT 'compound-eye' photosensor modules.

detector:icarus-t600.name: ICARUS T600

summary.plain: A 760-tonne liquid argon detector, the first of its size ever built. It worked under an Italian mountain from 2010 to 2013, was rebuilt at CERN, and now sits at Fermilab as the far detector of a search for a possible fourth kind of neutrino.

detector:icarus-t600.technology: single-phase liquid argon time projection chamber in two adjacent modules

detector:icecube.name: IceCube in-ice array

detector:icecube.technology: In-ice Cherenkov array of digital optical modules frozen into the Antarctic ice sheet

detector:icecube-deepcore.technology: Densely instrumented in-ice Cherenkov infill at the centre of the IceCube array

detector:icetop.name: IceTop

summary.plain: The part of IceCube that sits on the snow surface: 81 pairs of frozen water tanks that catch the showers of particles made when cosmic rays hit the atmosphere. It also helps IceCube tell cosmic rays apart from neutrinos.

detector:icetop.technology: Surface array of ice-filled Cherenkov tanks read out by downward-facing digital optical modules

detector:ingrid.name: INGRID (T2K on-axis near detector)

summary.plain: A cross-shaped array of iron-and-scintillator modules sitting directly in the path of T2K's neutrino beam, 280 metres from where the beam is made. It checks that the beam is pointed the right way and has the expected shape, run after run.

detector:ingrid.technology: On-axis array of iron/scintillator sandwich modules that measures the neutrino beam direction and profile.

detector:l3.name: L3 detector

subsystems.name: Solenoid magnet

summary.plain: A detector at LEP's Point 2 built to measure electrons, muons and photons with exceptional precision, using dense bismuth-germanate crystals and one of the largest magnets ever built for a particle detector.

detector:l3.technology: Collider detector optimised for high-resolution electron, muon and photon measurement, built around a bismuth-germanate calorimeter and a very large solenoid magnet

detector:lz.name: LZ detector

detector:lz.technology: dual-phase (two-phase) liquid xenon time projection chamber

detector:microboone.name: MicroBooNE detector

detector:minerva.technology: finely segmented scintillator-strip tracker with electromagnetic and hadronic sampling calorimetry and passive nuclear targets

detector:miniboone.name: MiniBooNE detector

summary.plain: A 12-metre sphere holding 818 tonnes of clear mineral oil, watched by 1,520 light sensors, 541 metres from where Fermilab makes its Booster neutrino beam. Flashes of light reveal the particles a neutrino leaves behind.

detector:miniboone.technology: spherical mineral-oil Cherenkov and scintillation detector viewed by photomultiplier tubes

subsystems.description: 486 octagonal steel-scintillator planes arranged in two supermodules
subsystems.name: Octagonal planes

summary.plain: A 5,400-tonne stack of 486 eight-sided steel and plastic plates, magnetised so it could tell neutrinos from antineutrinos, sitting 705 metres underground in an old Minnesota iron mine 735 kilometres from the beam.

The 980-tonne little sister of the MINOS far detector, in a cavern 100 metres below Fermilab about a kilometre from where the neutrino beam is born. It recorded the beam before any neutrinos had changed type.

operating with the upgraded near detector

detector:nd280.name: ND280 (T2K off-axis near detector)

subsystems.description: Tracking planes of scintillating bars alternating with water-target/brass or lead foil, at the upstream end of the magnet.
subsystems.name: PØD (Pi-Zero Detector)

subsystems.description: Three gaseous time projection chambers interleaved with two fine-grained scintillator-bar detectors (FGDs), used to reconstruct charged-current interactions.
subsystems.name: Tracker (TPCs and FGDs)

subsystems.description: Surrounds the P0D and the tracker to detect gamma rays escaping the inner detectors.
subsystems.name: ECal (Electromagnetic Calorimeter)

subsystems.description: Scintillator instrumenting the return yoke of the magnet, measuring the range of muons exiting through the sides.
subsystems.name: SMRD (Side Muon Range Detector)

summary.plain: A stack of detectors inside a recycled particle-physics magnet, sitting just 280 metres from where T2K's neutrino beam is made. It measures the beam before the neutrinos have had a chance to change type, so physicists know what they started with.

detector:nd280.technology: Magnetized off-axis tracking detector: a water/brass Pi-Zero Detector (P0D), three gaseous time projection chambers and two fine-grained scintillator detectors as the tracker, surrounded by an electromagnetic calorimeter, all inside the recycled UA1 dipole magnet instrumented as a side muon range detector (SMRD).

detector:nova-far-detector.name: NOvA far detector

subsystems.description: 344,000 cells of extruded, highly reflective plastic PVC filled with liquid scintillator (both NOvA detectors together)
subsystems.name: PVC cell array

summary.plain: A 14,000-tonne block of plastic tubes filled with a liquid that flashes when particles pass through, sitting on the surface in northern Minnesota. It catches the few neutrinos that survive an 810-kilometre trip from Chicago.

detector:nova-far-detector.technology: segmented tracking calorimeter of extruded PVC cells filled with liquid scintillator, read out by avalanche photodiodes

detector:nova-near-detector.name: NOvA near detector

summary.plain: A small copy of the NOvA far detector, about 300 tonnes, sitting underground at Fermilab a kilometre from where the neutrino beam is made. It measures the beam before the neutrinos have had time to change type.

detector:nova-near-detector.technology: segmented tracking calorimeter of extruded PVC cells filled with liquid scintillator, functionally identical to the far detector

detector:opal.name: OPAL detector

specs.calorimeters: Calorimeters as a middle layer of the concentric detector
specs.muon_system: Muon detectors as the outermost layer of the concentric detector
specs.tracker: Tracking detectors nearest the beam pipe, part of the concentric 'onion' layout

subsystems.description: Tracking, calorimeter and muon-detector layers arranged concentrically around the beam pipe.
subsystems.name: Layered ('onion') structure

summary.plain: A roughly 12-metre cube built in layers like an onion, so that every kind of particle from a LEP collision was caught by the right layer: tracking near the beam, then calorimeters, then muon detectors on the outside.

detector:opal.technology: General-purpose collider detector with tracking, calorimeter and muon layers arranged concentrically around the beam pipe

intervals.label: construction and operation at the CERN Neutrino Platform

detector:protodune-dp.name: ProtoDUNE-DP

summary.plain: The second DUNE prototype at CERN. It tested a design in which the electron signal is amplified in a thin layer of argon gas above the liquid, allowing a much longer drift.

detector:protodune-dp.technology: dual-phase liquid argon time projection chamber with a single homogeneous drift volume and charge amplification in the gas phase

intervals.label: operation at the CERN Neutrino Platform

detector:protodune-sp.name: ProtoDUNE-SP

subsystems.description: Full-size DUNE APAs, three per anode plane, reading out the two drift volumes
subsystems.name: Anode plane assemblies

subsystems.description: External cosmic-ray tagger used together with the beam instrumentation
subsystems.name: Cosmic-ray tagger

summary.plain: A full-height prototype of the DUNE far detector, built at CERN and exposed to a test beam of known particles from 2018. It showed that the design works before the real detectors were built in South Dakota.

detector:protodune-sp.technology: single-phase liquid argon time projection chamber, a full-height prototype of the DUNE single-phase far detector module

detector:sbnd.name: SBND detector

summary.plain: A 112-tonne liquid argon camera only 110 metres from where Fermilab makes its Booster neutrino beam. Being so close, it sees about 7,000 neutrinos a day, more than any similar detector.

detector:sbnd.technology: single-phase liquid argon time projection chamber

intervals.label: SK-II (half PMT density after the 2001 accident)

detector:super-kamiokande.name: Super-Kamiokande detector

subsystems.description: 11,129 inward-facing 20-inch (50 cm) PMTs covering about 40% of the wall, the world's largest PMTs at the time of installation.
subsystems.name: Inner Detector

subsystems.description: 1,885 outward-facing 8-inch PMTs used as a veto against incoming particles and for shielding characterisation.
subsystems.name: Outer Detector

subsystems.description: Gadolinium sulfate dissolved in the ultra-pure water from 2020 to tag neutron captures, improving sensitivity to inverse-beta-decay signals such as supernova relic neutrinos.
subsystems.name: SK-Gd upgrade

summary.plain: A cylindrical tank 39 metres across and 41 metres tall, filled with 50,000 tonnes of ultra-clean water and lined with more than eleven thousand light-sensing tubes, sitting a kilometre underground near Kamioka.

detector:super-kamiokande.technology: Cylindrical stainless-steel tank of ultra-pure water instrumented with inward- and outward-facing photomultiplier tubes, optically separated into an inner and an outer detector.

detector:ua1.name: UA1 detector

specs.calorimeters: 48 lead-layer electromagnetic subdetectors nicknamed 'gondolas', plus hadronic calorimetry
specs.muon_system: Muon chambers requiring about 30 km of extruded aluminium
specs.tracker: Six-chambered central imaging drift chamber, 5.8 m long and 2.3 m in diameter - the largest imaging drift chamber of its day

subsystems.description: Six-chambered cylinder 5.8 m long and 2.3 m in diameter; the largest imaging drift chamber of its day.
subsystems.name: Central imaging drift chamber

subsystems.description: An 800-tonne conventional electromagnet surrounding the central detector.
subsystems.name: Dipole magnet

summary.plain: A house-sized detector wrapped around the SPS beam pipe, with a giant electronic 'camera' (a drift chamber) at its heart to photograph particle tracks from each collision.

detector:ua1.technology: General-purpose (4-pi) collider detector with a central imaging drift chamber, electromagnetic and hadronic calorimetry and muon chambers around a conventional dipole magnet

detector:ua2.name: UA2 detector

specs.calorimeters: Complete electromagnetic and hadronic calorimetry down to about 5 degrees from the beam
specs.muon_system: None: UA2 had no muon detector
specs.tracker: 6,096 independent silicon dE/dx counters; scintillating-fibre tracker (SFD) added in the 1985-1987 upgrade, followed by a silicon pad detector

subsystems.description: Complete calorimetric coverage down to about 5 degrees from the beam line, used for electron and jet identification and energy measurement.
subsystems.name: Electromagnetic and hadronic calorimetry

subsystems.description: A scintillating-fibre tracker added in the 1985-1987 upgrade to improve tracking and electron identification.
subsystems.name: Scintillating fibre detector (SFD)

summary.plain: A detector built almost entirely from calorimeters, layered like an onion around the beam pipe, that measured energy rather than bending particle tracks in a magnet.

detector:ua2.technology: Non-magnetic, highly segmented electromagnetic and hadronic calorimeter with a scintillating-fibre tracker added in 1985-1987

experiment:aleph.energy_regime: Electron-positron collisions at and above the Z resonance (about 91 GeV, rising to 200 GeV from 1995)
experiment:aleph.name: ALEPH

summary.plain: One of four giant detectors on CERN's LEP electron-positron collider from 1989 to 2000, used to study the Z and W bosons with great precision, including proving there are exactly three kinds of light neutrino.

aliases: Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array
experiment:amanda.energy_regime: Atmospheric and astrophysical neutrinos with typical reconstructed energies of several hundred GeV and above
experiment:amanda.name: AMANDA

summary.plain: The pioneering telescope that froze light sensors into the ice at the South Pole to catch neutrinos. It proved the idea worked and was later absorbed into its much bigger successor, IceCube.

experiment:atlas.energy_regime: Proton-proton collisions at 7-13.6 TeV centre-of-mass energy; lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair
experiment:atlas.name: ATLAS

summary.plain: ATLAS is one of the two big general-purpose experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Its 7000-tonne detector sits in a cavern 100 metres underground and records what comes out of proton collisions. In 2012 ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson.

experiment:belle.energy_regime: e+e- collisions at the Υ(4S) resonance, √s ≈ 10.58 GeV
experiment:belle.name: Belle

summary.plain: An experiment at the KEK laboratory in Japan that ran from 1999 to 2010. It watched electrons and positrons collide to make pairs of B particles, and showed that matter and antimatter behave differently — work that led to the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The successor to the Belle experiment at the KEK laboratory in Japan. Running since 2019, it records electron-positron collisions from the SuperKEKB machine, looking for tiny departures from the known laws of physics in the decays of heavy, short-lived particles.

experiment:cms.energy_regime: Proton-proton (and heavy-ion) collisions at TeV centre-of-mass energies: designed for 14 TeV, 13.6 TeV delivered in LHC Run 3
experiment:cms.name: CMS

summary.plain: One of the two big general-purpose experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Thousands of scientists use it to photograph the debris of proton collisions 40 million times a second. In 2012 it was one of the two experiments that found the Higgs boson.

aliases: Detector with Lepton, Photon and Hadron Identification
experiment:delphi.energy_regime: Electron-positron collisions at and above the Z resonance (about 91 GeV, rising to 209 GeV by 2000)
experiment:delphi.name: DELPHI

summary.plain: One of four giant detectors on CERN's LEP electron-positron collider from 1989 to 2000, known for its Ring Imaging Cherenkov detectors that could identify the type of each charged particle produced.

experiment:dune.energy_regime: GeV-scale accelerator neutrinos (wide band, 60-120 GeV protons), plus MeV-scale supernova neutrinos

intervals.label: DUNE collaboration formed from LBNE and LBNO

experiment:dune.name: Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment

summary.plain: A very large experiment that will send neutrinos 1285 kilometres through the Earth from Illinois to South Dakota, where detectors filled with liquid argon a mile underground will record them. It aims to find out whether neutrinos and antineutrinos behave differently, to catch neutrinos from an exploding star, and to look for protons decaying.

The next, much bigger version of Super-Kamiokande, being built in a newly dug cavern near the original detector. When it starts up later this decade it will use the same J-PARC neutrino beam and look for a difference between how neutrinos and antineutrinos behave, hunt for proton decay, and watch for supernovae.

The first big liquid-argon neutrino detector ever built. It ran under an Italian mountain from 2010-2013, was rebuilt at CERN, and now sits at Fermilab as the far detector in a hunt for a possible fourth kind of neutrino.

experiment:icecube.energy_regime: About 10 GeV (DeepCore threshold) to the PeV scale and above for in-ice neutrinos; 300 TeV to 1 EeV cosmic rays with IceTop
experiment:icecube.name: IceCube

summary.plain: A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice at the South Pole turned into a telescope. More than five thousand light sensors frozen deep in the ice catch the faint flashes made when a neutrino from space crashes into the ice.

The planned successor to IceCube: about eight times the volume of ice, ten thousand light sensors and a huge radio antenna array, designed to catch many more neutrinos and the most energetic ones of all.

New, more sensitive light detectors added to the middle of IceCube. They let the observatory see lower-energy neutrinos more sharply and help scientists understand the ice itself, which improves every measurement IceCube has already made.

aliases: KEK to Kamioka long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment
experiment:k2k.name: K2K (KEK to Kamioka)

summary.plain: The world's first long-baseline neutrino experiment: a beam of neutrinos made at KEK's proton accelerator was sent 250 km through the Earth to the Super-Kamiokande detector, to check whether the atmospheric neutrino puzzle Super-K had already seen was really neutrino oscillation.

quantity.display: 4500 t total (680-1040 t fiducial, depending on analysis)

summary.plain: A tank of water deep in a Japanese mine, built in 1983 to look for protons decaying. It never saw one, but in February 1987 it caught a handful of neutrinos from a supernova exploding in a nearby galaxy - the first time anyone had detected neutrinos from a star other than the Sun.

experiment:l3.energy_regime: Electron-positron collisions at and above the Z resonance (about 91 GeV, rising to 209 GeV by 2000)
experiment:l3.name: L3

summary.plain: One of four giant detectors on CERN's LEP electron-positron collider from 1989 to 2000, built to measure electrons, muons and photons with exceptional precision using bismuth-germanate crystals and a huge magnet.

LUX was a dark matter detector holding about a third of a tonne of liquid xenon, run from 2013 to 2016 in the same underground hall in South Dakota that LZ uses now. It found no dark matter, and set the tightest limits of its day.

experiment:lz.energy_regime: keV-scale nuclear recoils from WIMPs of a few GeV/c2 to hundreds of TeV/c2
experiment:lz.name: LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ)

summary.plain: LZ is a dark matter experiment a mile underground in South Dakota. It watches seven tonnes of liquid xenon for the tiny flash of light expected if a dark matter particle hits a xenon nucleus. It began taking data at the end of 2021 and has seen no such particle so far.

A 170-tonne liquid-argon camera on Fermilab's Booster neutrino beam, built to find out what caused an earlier experiment's mysterious signal, and along the way to measure neutrino collisions with unprecedented clarity.
A compact, finely sliced detector at Fermilab that measured exactly how neutrinos bounce off different atomic nuclei, data that other neutrino experiments need to interpret their own results.

A Fermilab experiment built to settle a puzzling result from an earlier Los Alamos experiment. It watched a beam of neutrinos with a 12-metre sphere of mineral oil from 2002 to 2019, and saw its own unexplained excess of signals.

experiment:minos.energy_regime: On-axis NuMI νμ-dominated beam, peak energy about 3 GeV
experiment:minos.name: MINOS

summary.plain: A neutrino experiment that sent Fermilab's beam 735 kilometres underground to an old iron mine in Minnesota, comparing what arrived to what was measured near the source, from 2005 to 2012.
MINOS's second act: the same two detectors kept running from 2013 to 2016 on a higher-energy beam, hunting for a hypothetical fourth kind of neutrino.

experiment:nova.energy_regime: Off-axis NuMI wide-band beam peaked at 1.8 GeV
experiment:nova.name: NOvA

summary.plain: A long-distance neutrino experiment: Fermilab fires a beam of neutrinos 810 kilometres through the Earth to northern Minnesota, watching how they change type on the way to learn about neutrino masses and matter-antimatter asymmetry.

experiment:opal.energy_regime: Electron-positron collisions at and above the Z resonance (about 91 GeV, rising to 209 GeV by 2000)

quantity.display: ~12 m long x 12 m high x 12 m wide

experiment:opal.name: OPAL

summary.plain: One of four giant detectors on CERN's LEP electron-positron collider from 1989 to 2000, built as a layered, general-purpose apparatus about the size of a house to catch every kind of particle from the collisions.

The newest and closest of Fermilab's three short-baseline liquid-argon detectors, sitting right next to where the neutrino beam is made so it can measure the beam before anything has a chance to change.

intervals.label: SK-II (half PMT density after the 2001 accident)

summary.plain: A tank of 50,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water, a kilometre under a mountain near Kamioka, watched by more than eleven thousand light sensors. It caught the first solid evidence that neutrinos change type as they travel, has watched the Sun in neutrinos for decades, and is the distant target for neutrino beams fired from J-PARC.

intervals.label: first T2K neutrino event observed at Super-Kamiokande
shutdown after the Great East Japan Earthquake
shutdown after the J-PARC hadron-hall radiation accident
T2K-II: operation with the upgraded ND280 and 760 kW beam

summary.plain: A beam of neutrinos made at the J-PARC accelerator in Tokai, on Japan's Pacific coast, is aimed 295 km across the country at the Super-Kamiokande detector under a mountain near Kamioka. By comparing what arrives with what was sent, T2K found that muon neutrinos turn into electron neutrinos, and is now comparing neutrinos with antineutrinos.

experiment:ua1.energy_regime: Proton-antiproton collisions at 540-630 GeV centre-of-mass energy
experiment:ua1.name: UA1

summary.plain: A giant particle detector built around CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron in the early 1980s, when the machine was turned into a proton-antiproton collider. UA1 co-discovered the W and Z bosons, the carriers of the weak nuclear force.

experiment:ua2.energy_regime: Proton-antiproton collisions at 540-630 GeV centre-of-mass energy
experiment:ua2.name: UA2

summary.plain: A particle detector built around CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron in the early 1980s, alongside UA1, when the machine was turned into a proton-antiproton collider. UA2 co-discovered the W and Z bosons using precise calorimeters rather than a magnetic spectrometer.

facility:amundsen-scott-south-pole-stati.name: Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station
facility:amundsen-scott-south-pole-stati.operator_text: U.S. National Science Foundation / U.S. Antarctic Program

summary.plain: The United States research station at the South Pole. It is the southernmost place people live all year, and it supports the giant IceCube neutrino telescope buried in the ice below it.

aliases: Organisation européenne pour la recherche nucléaire
facility:cern.name: CERN
facility:cern.operator_text: CERN, European Organization for Nuclear Research

summary.plain: CERN is Europe's particle physics laboratory, on the Swiss-French border near Geneva. Founded in 1954 by twelve countries, it builds and runs the accelerators that send beams of protons and ions into experiments such as ATLAS and CMS, and it is the home of the Large Hadron Collider.

facility:fermilab.name: Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory
facility:fermilab.operator_text: Fermi Research Alliance, LLC for the U.S. Department of Energy

summary.plain: The United States national laboratory for particle physics, near Chicago. It builds and runs the chain of machines that produce the most intense beams of neutrinos in the world, and it hosts the DUNE experiment.

facility:j-parc.name: J-PARC (Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex)
facility:j-parc.operator: Operated jointly by the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) and the High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK)
facility:j-parc.operator_text: Operated jointly by the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) and the High Energy Accelerator Research Organization (KEK)

summary.plain: A large proton accelerator laboratory on the Pacific coast of Japan, run jointly by two national research organisations. Its most powerful machine drives a beam of neutrinos across the country to detectors in the mountains of western Japan.

facility:kamioka-observatory.name: Kamioka Observatory (ICRR, University of Tokyo)
facility:kamioka-observatory.operator: Institute for Cosmic Ray Research, University of Tokyo
facility:kamioka-observatory.operator_text: Institute for Cosmic Ray Research, University of Tokyo

summary.plain: An underground laboratory inside a mine in the Japanese Alps, a kilometre beneath a mountain. The rock above screens out most cosmic rays, so very rare signals from neutrinos can be seen.

aliases: National Laboratory for High Energy Physics

intervals.label: National Laboratory for High Energy Physics

facility:kek.name: KEK (High Energy Accelerator Research Organization)
facility:kek.operator: Inter-University Research Institute Corporation High Energy Accelerator Research Organization
facility:kek.operator_text: Inter-University Research Institute Corporation High Energy Accelerator Research Organization

summary.plain: Japan's national accelerator laboratory at Tsukuba, founded in 1971. Its 12 GeV proton accelerator made the first long-distance beam of neutrinos ever aimed at a detector hundreds of kilometres away.

The largest underground research laboratory in the world, built beside a motorway tunnel under the Gran Sasso mountain in central Italy. About 1400 metres of rock overhead cut the shower of cosmic particles by a factor of a million, which lets very quiet experiments run there.

aliases: Soudan Underground Mine State Park laboratory

intervals.label: MINOS far detector hall in operation

facility:soudan-underground-laboratory.name: Soudan Underground Laboratory

summary.plain: A laboratory dug into a disused iron mine in northern Minnesota, about 700 metres below ground. The rock above it screens out most of the particles raining down from the sky, which let it host the far detector of the MINOS neutrino experiment and a dark matter search.

intervals.label: South Dakota Science and Technology Authority formed

facility:surf.name: Sanford Underground Research Facility
facility:surf.operator_text: South Dakota Science and Technology Authority

summary.plain: A laboratory built in a former gold mine in Lead, South Dakota. Nearly a mile of rock above it blocks cosmic rays, so experiments there can look for very rare events, including the giant DUNE neutrino detectors.

site:ash-river-nova-far-detector.name: Ash River NOvA far detector laboratory

summary.plain: A large surface building in the forest near Ash River, Minnesota, close to the Canadian border. It holds the NOvA far detector, 810 kilometres from the neutrino beam at Fermilab, with only a thin layer of concrete and heavy mineral above it.

The underground cavern at Point 2 of the LEP ring, near the French village of Sergy, where the L3 detector recorded electron-positron collisions from 1989 to 2000. The same cavern and L3's huge magnet were later reused for the ALICE experiment.
The underground cavern at Point 4 of the LEP ring, near the French village of Echenevex, where the ALEPH detector recorded electron-positron collisions from 1989 to 2000.

The underground cavern at Point 8 of the LEP ring, near the French town of Ferney-Voltaire, where the DELPHI detector recorded electron-positron collisions from 1989 to 2000. The same cavern now houses the LHCb experiment.

CERN's main campus, an 80-hectare site that straddles the Swiss-French border next to the village of Meyrin outside Geneva. Most of the laboratory's offices, workshops, computer centre and visitor buildings are here, and the ATLAS experiment sits underground at its edge.
A large hall at CERN, on the French side of the laboratory, where full-size prototypes of the DUNE detectors were built and tested in a particle beam.

The underground cavern at the edge of CERN's Meyrin campus where the ATLAS detector sits, about 100 metres below ground. It is one of the eight access points around the 27-kilometre Large Hadron Collider ring and the place where two of the LHC's proton beams are made to collide inside ATLAS.
The place where the CMS experiment sits: a cavern about 100 metres below the village of Cessy in France, on the ring of the Large Hadron Collider just across the border from Geneva.
The underground hall on CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron ring where the UA2 detector sat to catch head-on collisions between protons and antiprotons.
The underground hall on CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron ring where the UA1 detector sat to catch head-on collisions between protons and antiprotons.
The 27-square-kilometre laboratory site west of Chicago where Fermilab accelerators, the neutrino beamlines and the DUNE near detector are located.
The J-PARC laboratory site on the Pacific coast at Tokai, about 115 km north-east of Tokyo, where the proton accelerators and the neutrino beam target are.

site:j-parc-neutrino-near-detector-hall.name: J-PARC neutrino near detector hall (280 m)

summary.plain: An underground pit on the J-PARC site, 280 metres from the target where the neutrinos are made. It holds the detectors that measure the beam before the neutrinos have had time to change type.

depth.display: 650 m of rock at the detector centre

summary.plain: A newly excavated cavern 600 metres underground in the Tochibora part of the Kamioka mine, about 8 kilometres from Super-Kamiokande, being prepared for the much larger Hyper-Kamiokande detector.
A cavern a kilometre inside a mountain in the Mozumi mine near Hida, Gifu. It holds the Super-Kamiokande water tank, reached by a horizontal tunnel from the valley.

The collision hall on the KEK laboratory campus in Tsukuba, Japan, where the electron and positron beams of the KEKB and SuperKEKB rings are brought together and where the Belle and Belle II detectors have stood.
One of three big rooms carved out of the rock under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy, about 100 metres long. The ICARUS liquid-argon detector stood at its northern end from 2010 to 2013.
The purpose-built cavern half a mile underground in the old Soudan iron mine that held the MINOS far detector, 735 kilometres from the neutrino beam that was aimed at it.
The patch of Antarctic ice next to the South Pole station where a cubic kilometre of sensors is frozen in, between about 1.5 and 2.5 kilometres below the surface.

site:surf-4850-level-dune-far-detector.name: SURF 4850 Level — LBNF/DUNE far detector caverns

summary.plain: Caverns nearly a mile underground at the Sanford laboratory, excavated to hold the huge liquid-argon detectors of the DUNE experiment.

site:surf-davis-campus-lz.name: Davis Campus, 4850 Level, Sanford Underground Research Facility

summary.plain: A laboratory hall about 1.5 kilometres below the surface in a former gold mine in Lead, South Dakota. It was dug in the 1960s for Ray Davis's experiment that counted neutrinos from the Sun, and it now houses the LZ dark matter detector.

site:surf-surface-campus.name: SURF Surface Campus, Lead, South Dakota

summary.plain: The above-ground part of the Sanford laboratory in Lead, South Dakota, with the shafts, offices and assembly buildings that serve the experiments a mile below.
